questions.q: The first sign of a signalling/train control failure at Operations Control Centre (OCC) is typically:
options: Loss of train detection or indications, or European Train Control System (ETCS)/Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) failure indications on the Operations Control Centre (OCC) screens
A passenger complaint about delays
A failure of the station lighting
The depot asking for a train
questions.explain: Detection and indication loss on the control screens is how the failure announces itself.

questions.q: On detecting a signalling failure, the immediate protective action is to:
options: Speed up trains to clear the area quickly
Let trains continue on the timetable
Switch off all station announcements
Stop or hold trains at stations or safe points in the affected area
questions.explain: Protect first — trains are held at safe points before anything is diagnosed in detail.

questions.q: After trains are held, the next step in a signalling failure is to:
options: Resume normal working at once
Identify the failed boundary — which section, which equipment, and which trains are inside it
Cancel the whole day's service
Send all passengers home
questions.explain: You cannot authorise degraded working until you know exactly what has failed and who is affected.

questions.q: Degraded working during a signalling failure means trains:
options: Run normally because drivers can see the track
Run faster to make up lost time
Proceed in the prescribed restricted mode under Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorisation, at restricted speed with increased spacing
Run without any authorisation if the line looks clear
questions.explain: Restricted speed plus bigger gaps replace the failed automatic protection.

questions.q: A manual train movement in a failed-signalling area requires:
options: Authority as per the rule book — written or verbal with read-back — before moving
Only the driver's confidence
A nod from a platform staff member
The passengers' agreement
questions.explain: Authority with read-back is the substitute for the missing signals — no authority, no movement.

questions.q: In the affected section during degraded signalling working, the usual rule is:
options: As many trains as can fit
Only one train in the affected section at a time, as prescribed
Two trains if both drivers agree
Trains at normal headway
questions.explain: One train in the section removes the collision risk that signalling normally manages.

questions.q: Why is speed restricted during manual/degraded signalling working?
options: To save electricity during the failure
Because passengers dislike fast trains
To give engineers time to reach the site
Without automatic protection, the driver needs distance and time to stop on sight and on instructions
questions.explain: Restricted speed is the human replacement for Automatic Train Protection (ATP) — stopping distance must stay inside visible, authorised space.

questions.q: If a signalling failure is total in an area, the correct decision is to:
options: Run trains on drivers' judgement alone
Close the entire network permanently
Suspend service in the affected area and apply manual working rules until engineers certify restoration
Wait one hour and resume automatically
questions.explain: Total failure means no safe degraded mode — suspension plus certified restoration is the rule.

questions.q: During a signalling failure, stations and passengers must be given:
options: No information until the failure is repaired
Delay information, with extra staff sent to key stations
Only the technical fault codes
Free tickets for the next day
questions.explain: Information and extra hands at stations are part of the failure response, not an afterthought.

questions.q: Restoration after a signalling failure is done:
options: In stages — reset/repair, a test movement at caution, then a step back up to normal headway
Instantly at full speed and normal headway
Only after a full day's closure
By the first passenger train at line speed
questions.explain: Staged restoration proves the system before trusting it with a full service.

questions.q: Who certifies that signalling is fit before normal working resumes?
options: The first train driver to pass through
The station master on duty alone
The responsible signalling engineer/controller — resumption without certification is prohibited
Any technician who was nearby
questions.explain: The 'declared fit' gate applies to signalling exactly as to track and power.

questions.q: A train is inside the failed section when the failure occurs. It should:
options: Continue to its destination at normal speed
Reverse out of the section on the driver's decision
Open doors and detrain passengers at once
Stop or proceed only as instructed by Operations Control Centre (OCC) under the degraded rules
questions.explain: Trains inside the failure are moved one instruction at a time under Operations Control Centre (OCC) control.

questions.q: Read-back of a verbal movement authority is essential because:
options: It proves the driver received the exact authority — limits, section and conditions — without error
It fills the radio channel so others cannot speak
It is a formality with no safety value
It replaces the need for Operations Control Centre (OCC) to log the authority
questions.explain: A misheard authority can send a train into an occupied section — read-back catches the error.

questions.q: Which is a correct cause-and-response pair for signalling failure?
options: Loss of train detection — increase frequency
Loss of train detection — open all Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) permanently
Loss of train detection — hold trains, identify the boundary, authorise degraded working
Loss of train detection — evacuate all stations at once
questions.explain: The response scales with the failure: protect, identify, degrade, restore.

questions.q: Platform Screen Doors are affected by a signalling failure because:
options: Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) run on an unrelated system with no link at all
Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) are integrated with signalling/train control — their operation must be managed under the degraded procedure
Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) cause signalling failures
Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) must be removed during failures
questions.explain: Platform Screen Door (PSD)-signalling integration is a Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) feature — a signalling failure plan always includes the doors.

questions.q: During degraded working, headway between trains will:
options: Decrease to clear the backlog
Stay exactly as in the normal timetable
Become zero at stations
Increase — trains run further apart than normal
questions.explain: Wider spacing is the price of manual protection — capacity falls, safety holds.

questions.q: A driver in a degraded-working section receives conflicting instructions from two sources. He should:
options: Follow the most recent voice he heard
Follow whichever instruction is faster
Stop and seek clarification from Operations Control Centre (OCC) — the single controlling authority
Decide himself and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) later
questions.explain: One controlling authority prevents conflicting movements — doubt means stop and ask.

questions.q: Why are extra staff sent to key stations during a long signalling failure?
options: To repair the signalling equipment themselves
To manage crowds, give information and assist with manual procedures at stations
To sell tickets for bus services
To close the stations early
questions.explain: Failures are managed at stations as much as on the track — people and information need hands.

questions.q: The correct order for handling a signalling failure is:
options: Detect, protect (hold trains), identify the boundary, authorise degraded working, inform, restore in stages
Authorise movements, detect, protect, restore, inform
Restore, inform, detect, identify, protect
Inform passengers, resume service, identify the fault later
questions.explain: This sequence mirrors the flowchart: protection before diagnosis, diagnosis before movement.

questions.q: A signalling failure affects only one section. Service on the rest of the line should:
options: Stop everywhere for the whole day
Run into the failed section as normal
Be replaced entirely by buses at once
Continue, regulated around the affected section with short-turns as needed
questions.explain: Failures are contained — the healthy network keeps running around the protected area.

questions.q: What does 'manual working' replace during a signalling failure?
options: The need for drivers in trains
The automatic detection and authority system — replaced by human authority, restricted speed and spacing
The passenger information system
The traction power supply
questions.explain: Manual working is the rule-book fallback when the automatic system cannot protect movements.

questions.q: A test movement after signalling repair is run at caution mainly to:
options: Prove the restored equipment works correctly before normal speeds and headways return
Give passengers a slow scenic trip
Check the train's catering stock
Train a new driver
questions.explain: The first movement is an experiment under control — its success authorises the step up.

questions.q: During a signalling failure at night with few passengers, the safety rules:
options: Can be relaxed as the risk is low
Allow normal speed on sight
Remain exactly the same — degraded working does not relax with low traffic
Allow drivers to self-authorise movements
questions.explain: Low traffic reduces consequences, not the rules — protection standards never depend on crowd size.

questions.q: If the signalling failure also causes loss of Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s view of train positions, Operations Control Centre (OCC) should:
options: Assume trains are where the timetable says
Continue normal working from memory
Ask passengers to report train positions
Treat it as more serious — rely on reports from trains/stations and restrict movements further
questions.explain: Losing detection removes Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s eyes — uncertainty always means more restriction, never less.

questions.q: Which information is most important when logging a signalling failure?
options: Time, affected section/equipment, trains held, authorities issued and restoration certification
The names of delayed passengers
The weather at the time
The number of announcements made
questions.explain: The log must let an enquiry rebuild the event — times, boundaries, authorities and the fit declaration.

questions.q: A passenger train approaches a section where signalling has just failed, but its own signals appear normal. The driver should:
options: Proceed at full speed since his signals look fine
Obey Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s instructions for the affected area — local appearance does not override control information
Stop permanently and detrain passengers
Ignore Operations Control Centre (OCC) as the train is unaffected
questions.explain: Failures can be partial and deceptive — Operations Control Centre (OCC) holds the complete picture.

questions.q: Bus bridging is most likely to be arranged during a signalling failure when:
options: The failure lasts five minutes
Passengers ask for a road trip
A single train is delayed slightly
The failure is prolonged and the affected section cannot sustain even degraded rail service
questions.explain: Buses replace trains only when degraded rail working cannot carry the load for a long period.

questions.q: After restoration, why is headway built back gradually instead of restoring the full timetable at once?
options: Drivers need rest between trips
Passengers prefer fewer trains
Trains are out of position and the system must be proven stable — a phased build-up avoids a second collapse
The timetable office opens late
questions.explain: Phased restoration is itself a safety and stability procedure.

questions.q: In Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS), the train control involved in such failures includes:
options: Token block working only
European Train Control System (ETCS)-based signalling with Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) supervision at Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Semaphore signals only
Hand flags as the normal system
questions.explain: Namo Bharat runs on European Train Control System (ETCS) over Long Term Evolution (LTE) with Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) at Operations Control Centre (OCC) — its failure handling follows that system.

questions.q: The single most dangerous action during a signalling failure would be:
options: Allowing trains to run at normal speed on drivers' own judgement without authority
Holding trains at stations
Informing passengers about delays
Sending extra staff to stations
questions.explain: Unauthorised normal-speed running removes every layer of protection at once.

questions.q: A Signal Passed At Danger (SPAD) occurs during degraded working. The train involved must:
options: Continue slowly to the next station
Stop, and not move again without fresh authority from the Operations Control Centre (OCC); the event is reported and treated as a serious incident
Reverse back behind the signal on its own
Wait five minutes and proceed
questions.explain: A Signal Passed At Danger (SPAD) means the last safety barrier was crossed. The train stops, the Operations Control Centre (OCC) takes charge, and the case is investigated — never covered up by moving on.

questions.q: A track circuit fails and shows a section 'occupied' although no train is confirmed there. Until the section is proved clear, it must be treated as:
options: Clear, because the indication is probably false
Occupied — trains may enter only one at a time, on written/verbal authority with read-back, at restricted speed
Open for normal automatic working
Closed permanently
questions.explain: A failed track circuit cannot prove the section is empty, so the safe assumption is 'occupied'. Movements continue cautiously on authority, exactly as if a train were standing there.

questions.q: During a signalling failure, a set of points (the movable rails that change a train's route) must be passed over by trains. Before any train uses them, the points must be:
options: Painted a bright colour
Clamped and locked in the required position, and the clamping verified
Left free so they can move if needed
Oiled by the driver
questions.explain: With powered operation and detection lost, a clamp physically locks the points so they cannot move under a train. Clamp, lock, verify — then authorise the movement.

questions.q: With automatic signalling dead on a double-line section, the degraded method that keeps movements safe is based on the absolute-block principle, which means:
options: Trains follow each other closely at sight
Only one train is allowed in the section between two stations at a time, admitted on authority from the receiving end
Trains run on the wrong line freely
The fastest train gets the section first
questions.explain: Absolute block is the oldest and safest degraded rule: one section, one train. Capacity falls sharply, but two trains can never be sent into the same space.

questions.q: Where signals themselves cannot be used during a failure, authorised staff at the spot guide trains using:
options: Hand signals — flags by day and lamps by night — shown from a position where the driver can clearly see them
Whistles only
Mobile phone torches waved randomly
Shouting from the platform end
questions.explain: Hand signals are the human backup of the signal system: a green flag or lamp authorises movement, red stops it. The signaller stands where the driver cannot miss the indication.
